Perhaps the most striking of these was the close internal connection between the philosophical outlook and the religious spirit of the school.
This led some Eastern and Orientalist researchers to see Shiʿi philosophy as having a mystical character.
But what appears to be mystical in it comes, in our view, from the deep absorption of Shiʿi thought in the doctrine of the infallibility of the Imams.

That devotion, together with the tragic historical conditions faced by the Shiʿi movement at different stages of its history, gave Shiʿi philosophical thought an unusually strong emotional intensity. This is what gave it the character that sometimes brings it close to mysticism.
Here we mean the Twelver Imami Shiʿa in particular, rather than the Ismailis or other Shiʿi groups.
Most of the critical discussion so far has focused on earlier writers who worked directly in intellectual fields such as logic, theology, philosophy, or legal theory.
We have discussed historians only when a particular historian also took part in historical theory or the philosophy of history, as in the cases of Ibn Khaldūn and al-Shahrastānī.

We therefore need to stop briefly and look at the attitudes of earlier Arab-Islamic historians themselves. Their surviving works recorded many features of medieval Arab-Islamic society during the period in which this intellectual heritage was produced.
We should note, however, that most of these historical works are general histories of events, individuals, or countries.
Works devoted specifically to the history of intellectual life in general, or to one particular intellectual phenomenon, are relatively rare.
There is also a lack of works devoted specifically to the history of philosophy as a discipline in the sense in which we understand it today.

Al-Shahrastānī may have been almost alone in laying the foundations for a history of philosophy at the level possible in his own age, just as Ibn Khaldūn, in the Muqaddima, was almost alone in laying the foundations for a social science of history at the level possible in his.
But this does not mean that the historians of Arab-Islamic society ignored intellectual life, including philosophy.
In fact, some of their works come close to specialized histories of particular fields of thought.
Examples include the books known as works of biography and “classes”: classes of philosophers, physicians, poets, scholars of ḥadīth—that is, transmitters of reports about the Prophet—and others.
There were also books on religious sects and schools.

These are, in fact, historical records of an important part of intellectual life because they present the intellectual and theoretical principles behind the differences and disputes between the various sects and schools, including theological, legal-theoretical, and philosophical schools.

And even general historical works contain, to different degrees and with different levels of quality, records of intellectual events, movements, and developments, biographies of thinkers, and sometimes discussions of one field or another within Arab-Islamic thought.
Taken together, these historical writings therefore allow us to identify the ways in which Arab-Islamic historians approached the intellectual heritage that concerns us here.

● What stands out most clearly to the modern scientific researcher is that one approach dominates the way these historians looked at the heritage—that is, at the movement of intellectual life they were describing in their historical works.
It is a quantitative and fragmentary approach, something that can be seen as a historical form of what we would now call empiricism.
In the writings of these historians, intellectual events, movements, and currents appear as piles of separate episodes.
Events, periods, places, people, and situations accumulate one after another, but the internal relationships that connect them and turn them into broader historical patterns remain unseen.
The same is true of the external relationships through which these events and movements affect one another and are themselves affected.
Nor do these historians see how a gradual accumulation of quantitative changes can produce a qualitative transformation.

Their attention usually remains fixed on the outward course of each separate event, or on some side angle chosen by the historian that never reaches the deeper line running through the origin, development, and transformation of the larger historical process.
That side angle is often the reign of a caliph, the term of a governor, the rule of an emir, the command of a military leader, or a particular year marked by war, famine, or fitna.
Very often what they call fitna was actually a social revolt with deep causes that lay outside the way these historians understood the event.
They describe the war, the famine, or the fitna without discussing its deeper social causes.
This way of looking at intellectual activity naturally reflects the way these historians looked at the historical process in its more basic field: social life itself.
For historical reasons, they were unable to see realistically how social history develops or to identify the basic forces that decisively shape its direction in a particular society.

They were therefore also unable to see, first, the essential connection between intellectual activity and social activity and, second, the internal relationships between intellectual events and movements themselves.
● But this historical limitation does not explain every position taken by these historians.
It is true that a scientific understanding of historical development had not yet become possible in their age.
But in some cases that explanation is not enough.
We must also take account of personal motives, as well as objective class and ideological forces that shaped their positions.
We should not ignore the fact that many of them wrote history—whether political history or intellectual history—from the standpoint of the ruling power.
Some did so out of self-interest, some out of fear, some because they had absorbed the officially favoured ideology, and some simply because of their own class position.
One especially clear example is the attitude of earlier historians toward one of the most important historical crises faced by the Abbasid caliphate.

We mean the mass peasant uprising that spread across large sections of the peoples of the Arab-Islamic empire in Azerbaijan, northwestern Iran, and eastern Armenia at the beginning of the third Islamic century, during the reigns of al-Maʾmūn and al-Muʿtaṣim.
The uprising was led by Bābak al-Khurramī between 816 and 838 CE. It therefore became known as the Bābak revolt and remained active for twenty years, from 202 to 222 AH.

It so happens that the major Arabic historical sources for this period of Arab-Islamic society were written by historians who lived in the third and fourth Islamic centuries. Some of these historians lived through the Bābakī revolt themselves. Others wrote about the period while the events were still fresh. Yet in their major works, we find either silence about the revolt or a distorted picture of it—of its events, its aims, its ideology, and its social principles.

These distortions helped bury the revolt’s real character and obscure its radical social and intellectual dimensions. They came partly from the bias of these early historians, who sided with the caliphate, local rulers, and great feudal landowners—the very forces targeted by the revolt. In some cases, their own class background also shaped their views. And beyond this, they lacked the historical tools needed to uncover the social roots of this peasant uprising.

For one reason or another, most of them accepted the two-part historical deception spread by the authorities, their officials, and their allies, all of whom were threatened by the revolt’s aims. The revolt was presented, first, as an uprising against Islam and an expression of hostility toward the Arabs; and second, as a movement whose principles would destroy the moral order of society.
In general, these historians viewed the revolt from the standpoint of political authority and feudal ideology, though this bias took different forms in different writers.

Take al-Balādhurī, Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā (d. 279 AH/892 CE). He may well have witnessed the Bābakī revolt in his youth, or at least felt the intensity of a crisis that deeply troubled the caliphal court. Yet in his Conquests of the Lands, he virtually ignores it and gives it no direct treatment. The intellectual side of the movement appears only in a passing reference, where he calls Bābak, the leader of the revolt, “the unbelieving Khurramite.”

In doing so, he follows the same path as other writers who repeated accusations against the rebels without examining them, helping stir hostility toward them among Muslim populations throughout the Abbasid realm.

This position is hardly surprising when we remember al-Balādhurī’s close ties to the Abbasid caliphs and what is known of his habit of “seeking the company of men of rank and power.” Perhaps by remaining silent about the revolt and its social principles, he was keeping to himself an opinion that differed from the official one. He may have preferred silence rather than risk angering the very people whose favor he sought. Otherwise, it is difficult to explain why he said so little.

To his credit, however, al-Balādhurī gives us detailed reports about the way land was granted and controlled in the regions affected by the Khurramite revolt. He also describes the oppression suffered by the people of those areas, especially the peasants, at the hands of landholders, as well as the heavy taxes imposed by the caliphate and the harshness of its tax collectors. In this way, he provides us with evidence that helps reveal the social conditions that made the revolt inevitable.
Al-Yaʿqūbī, Aḥmad ibn Abī Yaʿqūb (d. after 284 AH), takes a somewhat different position in his well-known History.

The difference appears in two ways. First, he does not ignore the revolt, though he gives few details. Second, in the little he says about its ideology, he partly joins those who attack it, accusing the Bābakī rebels of plundering settlements, travelers, and pilgrims.

Even so, al-Yaʿqūbī and al-Balādhurī, together with al-Ṭabarī, Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Jarīr (224–310 AH), and al-Masʿūdī, Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn (d. 346 AH), did less than most of the historians discussed here to distort the real character of this peasant mass revolt.

With Ibn al-Nadīm, Abū al-Faraj Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq al-Warrāq (d. 385 AH/995 CE), the picture begins to grow darker. Myth and fact become increasingly tangled, until the myths themselves turn into “facts” in the works of the generation after Ibn al-Nadīm, then in those of later modern Arab researchers and Orientalists.

This continued until a contemporary Arab scholar confronted this whole obscuring tradition. He belongs to a new generation of researchers who are courageously opening the way toward studying our history and intellectual heritage through a scientific view of social history—historical materialism—and of the development of human thought within it.

This introduction cannot examine every position taken by the early writers toward the intellectual heritage we are studying. But the general survey above has shown the main trends in those positions and provided examples that reveal the intellectual and ideological assumptions behind them.
B — The Approaches of Modern Scholars
In the opening pages of this introduction, we placed the modern Arab return to its older heritage within the historical setting in which it began to take shape more than a century ago.

At that time, the return to the heritage was the intellectual expression of the changes that announced the beginning of the movement later called the “Arab Renaissance,” or Nahda. We traced this concern with the heritage back to the same forces that first produced the Nahda in its early, shallow form.

Later, a new form of the movement emerged from deeper popular currents within Arab society and from a broader social horizon. Its content changed. What had begun as a reformist “renaissance,” tied to the ambitions of leading Arab elites and to their indirect attempts to compromise with Western imperial ambitions, developed into a national liberation movement.
As the Arab movement changed, the idea of “returning to the heritage” changed with it.

At first, this return had the same renaissance character as the reformist Arab movement itself. In this form, it was close to romanticism. It looked back to the past simply because it was the past. It was driven by an emotional attachment to the past for its own sake and by a tendency to praise everything inherited from it without distinction or examination.
Earlier, we described this phenomenon through two qualities that seem contradictory: its content was reactionary, but its motives were progressive.

Its content was reactionary because it glorified the past without qualification. Its motives were progressive because it helped awaken national feeling and contributed to the revival of an Arab “identity” in the face of a double challenge: Turkish racialist Turanism on one side, and Western imperialism on the other, already preparing to divide the inheritance of the “sick man.”
At this stage, the movement back to the heritage took on the character suggested by the name commonly given to it: the “revival of the heritage.”
Literature—and especially poetry—was the first form this “revival” took.

But in reality, this was less a revival of the heritage than a draining away of what life still remained in it. Writers imitated its language, styles, images, and themes, but much of the living substance that had originally given those forms meaning was missing.

A new form of this “revival” then appeared. It was more useful and much closer to a real revival: the publication of old works in literature, criticism, poetry, history, law, and religious doctrine through the new technology of mechanical printing, which began spreading during the nineteenth century in countries such as Egypt, Lebanon, and Syria.
At first, however, these publishing efforts were largely unsystematic.
For one thing, books were usually chosen simply because the work or its author was famous. There was no broader principle guiding what should be published.

For another, publishers generally did not compare different manuscript copies of the same work in order to establish the most accurate text and date it properly, as Orientalist scholars were doing when they published works from the Arab-Islamic heritage.

There were probably several reasons for this weakness. Publishers often did not know the methods of scholarly manuscript editing. Many old manuscripts had also disappeared from Arab libraries because of repeated invasions and wars over many centuries. Another factor was the presence of Orientalists in Arab countries during and after the Crusades and their acquisition of a large share of the surviving manuscript heritage.

Even during this first stage of the return to the heritage, however, an important new movement appeared in the final third of the nineteenth century. It was new in its outlook and had a deep influence across the Muslim East: the school of Jamāl al-Dīn al-Afghānī (d. 1897) and his student Shaykh Muḥammad ʿAbduh (d. 1905).
Their approach to the heritage went beyond the almost romantic attitude that had dominated the period.

The Afghānī-ʿAbduh school approached the heritage with a degree of criticism. Al-Afghānī believed that the countries of the East needed to resist Western colonial ambitions with a form of thought freed from rigid and unquestioning reverence for the past.
The present, he believed, required a new understanding of inherited ideas—one that could help Eastern societies confront the growing danger of colonial domination.

From this starting point, al-Afghānī urged these societies to abandon inherited ideas and customs when they followed them blindly. He condemned the passivity and absolute fatalism that reached them under the name of divine decree and destiny.

This was the basis of his well-known attack on Sufis “who turn belief in divine decree and destiny into an excuse for sitting idle instead of earning a living.” He judged that people who understood trust in God as nothing more than passive dependence deserved to be humiliated and that society should be cleansed of their harmful influence, because their ideas did not agree with religion.

Muḥammad ʿAbduh, who represented the Arab-Egyptian wing of this school, worked from the same basic principle in his social and intellectual call to reinterpret the heritage of Islam—both doctrine and law—and the heritage of Muslim theologians and philosophers in the light of a modern world very different from the medieval one.

“Whoever follows the path of independent reasoning, does not rely on imitation in matters of belief, and is not protected from error may indeed make mistakes. But his error is accepted by God so long as the aim of his effort and the purpose of his careful examination are to reach the truth and arrive at certainty.”

The same outlook also kept Muḥammad ʿAbduh from following the traditionalist path of hostility toward the rationalist tradition represented by the Muʿtazila and the philosophers. Nor did he declare someone an unbeliever simply for believing in the eternity of the world.
He did not accept Sufism either, except when it took the form of “moral discipline guided by rational discipline.”
Nor did he side with reactionaries who said women should be denied education. He found it astonishing that people should be left trapped in ignorance and even encouraged to remain there.
He also rejected the inherited claim of strict jurists that Islam forbids sculpture and painting, and so on.

Even so, although the Afghānī-ʿAbduh school helped crack the wall of absolute reverence surrounding the heritage, it did not develop a method for studying that heritage that fundamentally broke with the older methods. It remained tied to the same ideological foundations on which those methods rested.
The first stage of the return to the heritage came to an end only when the movement itself began to take shape within the forces we analyzed at the beginning of this introduction.

By this we mean the growing transformations within the Arab national liberation movement: both its progressive content and the increasing maturity of the class and ideological struggles taking place inside the liberation movement itself.
In this new stage, the way people looked at the heritage began to acquire a progressive content on one level while becoming part of ideological struggle on another.

This change cannot be separated from the development of the Arab national liberation movement. But neither can it be separated from the growth of scientific knowledge among Arab researchers, their exposure to academic methods used in Western universities and Orientalist scholarship, and their growing familiarity with modern intellectual and philosophical currents emerging in developed capitalist societies.
For many, however, this opening toward outside knowledge remained one-sided. For some, it never went beyond a liberal outlook.
